subject: biology
title: Reproductive strategies
summary: Compares the main types of asexual reproduction with sexual reproduction, explains how each affects genetic diversity, and describes how reproductive cloning works and is used.
body:
Every species must reproduce to survive, but organisms do it in very different ways. Some simply copy themselves, while others combine genetic material from two parents. The strategy a species uses decides how fast it can multiply and how much genetic diversity its population has, which in turn affects how well it copes when its environment changes.

## Key ideas

### Asexual versus sexual reproduction

**Asexual reproduction** is the production of offspring from a single parent without the fusion of gametes. Offspring are produced by mitosis (or by binary fission in prokaryotes), so they are genetically identical to the parent and to each other, apart from any new mutations. A group of genetically identical individuals is called a **clone**.

**Sexual reproduction** is the production of offspring by the fusion of two **gametes** (sex cells, such as sperm and egg), usually from two different parents. Gametes are made by **meiosis**, a cell division that halves the chromosome number and shuffles alleles. Fusion of gametes at **fertilisation** forms a **zygote** with a full set of chromosomes. Offspring are genetically different from each other and from both parents.

### Types of asexual reproduction

- **Binary fission** — a prokaryotic cell (for example, a bacterium) copies its single circular chromosome, grows, and splits into two identical daughter cells. Under ideal conditions some bacteria divide every 20 minutes, so populations grow extremely quickly. Some single-celled eukaryotes such as *Amoeba* also split in two, but they use mitosis to divide their nucleus first.
- **Budding** — a small outgrowth (a bud) develops on the parent, grows, and eventually detaches as a new individual. Examples include yeast (a single-celled fungus) and *Hydra* (a small freshwater animal related to jellyfish).
- **Fragmentation** — the parent body breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a complete new organism. Examples include flatworms called planarians, some sea stars (if a piece includes part of the central disc) and filamentous algae.
- **Vegetative propagation** — new plants grow from non-reproductive parts of the parent such as stems, roots or leaves. Examples include runners (strawberries), tubers (potatoes), bulbs (onions) and rhizomes (many grasses). Humans use this deliberately when they take cuttings or graft plants.
- **Parthenogenesis** — an unfertilised egg develops into a new individual. It happens in aphids, some bees and ants (where unfertilised eggs become males), some lizards and, occasionally, in sharks and Komodo dragons kept without males. Because the egg comes from meiosis, parthenogenetic offspring are not always perfect copies of the mother, but their genetic variation is much lower than with sexual reproduction.

### Advantages and disadvantages

| | Asexual reproduction | Sexual reproduction |
|---|---|---|
| Number of parents | One — no need to find a mate | Usually two — energy spent finding and attracting mates |
| Speed | Fast; large numbers produced quickly | Slower; fewer offspring per unit of time |
| Energy cost | Low | High (gamete production, courtship, sometimes parental care) |
| Genetic diversity | Very low; offspring are clones | High; every offspring is unique |
| Best suited to | Stable, favourable environments | Changing or unpredictable environments |

The big drawback of asexual reproduction is lack of **genetic diversity** — the variety of alleles and allele combinations in a population. If a disease, predator or change in climate kills one individual, it is likely to kill them all, because they share the same genes. Sexual reproduction creates diversity in three main ways:

1. **Crossing over** in meiosis swaps sections between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations.
2. **Independent assortment** means each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up and separates independently, so gametes receive different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
3. **Random fertilisation** means any sperm can fuse with any egg.

With more variation, it is more likely that at least some individuals have traits that let them survive a new challenge. Those survivors reproduce, and the population persists. This is why many organisms that reproduce asexually, such as aphids, strawberries and many fungi, also reproduce sexually at certain times — they combine fast growth in good conditions with diversity when conditions change.

### Reproductive cloning

**Reproductive cloning** is the deliberate production of a whole new organism that is genetically identical to an existing one. In plants this is easy: cuttings, grafting and **tissue culture** (growing whole plants from small pieces of tissue on a sterile nutrient medium) all produce clones.

In mammals the main method is **somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT)**:

1. A body (somatic) cell is taken from the animal to be cloned (the donor).
2. An egg cell is taken from a female of the same species, and its nucleus is removed (it is enucleated).
3. The donor nucleus is inserted into the enucleated egg, or the whole donor cell is fused with it using a small electric pulse.
4. The reconstructed egg is stimulated to start dividing and grows into an early embryo.
5. The embryo is implanted into the uterus of a surrogate mother, who carries it to birth.

The offspring has the nuclear DNA of the donor, not of the egg provider or the surrogate. (It does carry mitochondrial DNA from the egg, so it is not 100% identical.) Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell this way.

Another method is **embryo splitting**, where an early embryo is divided into separate groups of cells that each develop into a genetically identical individual — like artificially made identical twins.

Uses of reproductive cloning include copying livestock or crop plants with valuable traits, producing large numbers of identical plants for horticulture and forestry, and helping to conserve endangered species. Limitations include a low success rate in animals, health problems in some clones, high cost, and the fact that cloned populations have no genetic diversity.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Growth by binary fission

A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells are present after 3 hours, assuming ideal conditions?

1. Number of divisions: 3 hours = 180 minutes; 180 ÷ 20 = 9 generations.
2. Each generation doubles the number, so cells = 2⁹.
3. 2⁹ = 512 cells.

All 512 cells are genetically identical except for any mutations. This shows why asexual reproduction is so effective at colonising a favourable environment quickly.

### Example 2: Diversity and disease

A banana grower plants a whole farm with one variety propagated from suckers (vegetative propagation). A fungal disease arrives that the variety is not resistant to. Predict the outcome and explain it.

1. Identify the reproduction type: suckers are vegetative propagation, so every plant is a clone.
2. Link to genetic diversity: the plants share the same alleles, including those that make them susceptible.
3. Predict: the disease is likely to spread through and damage the entire crop, because no plant carries a resistance allele.
4. Compare: a population produced sexually would be more likely to contain some resistant individuals that survive.

### Example 3: Identifying the parent of a clone

A nucleus from a skin cell of a black-faced sheep is inserted into an enucleated egg from a white-faced sheep, and the embryo is carried by a third, white-faced surrogate. The lamb has a black face, because its nuclear DNA, which controls the trait, came from the skin cell donor.

## Common mistakes

- Saying asexual offspring are always 100% identical. Mutations can occur, and SCNT clones carry the egg donor's mitochondrial DNA.
- Mixing up binary fission and mitosis. Binary fission is how prokaryotes divide; they do not have a nucleus or carry out mitosis.
- Thinking parthenogenesis involves fertilisation. It is development of an unfertilised egg.
- Believing a cloned animal is identical to its surrogate mother. The surrogate only carries the pregnancy.
- Writing that sexual reproduction is better in every way. It is costly and slow; its main advantage is genetic diversity.

## Exam tips

- When asked about advantages or disadvantages, link the feature to survival: for example, low diversity means the whole population may be wiped out by one disease.
- Name the specific processes that create diversity in sexual reproduction (crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation) rather than just saying it mixes genes.
- For SCNT questions, be able to trace which individual supplied which material and therefore what the offspring will look like.
- Use correct examples for each asexual type; vague answers such as plants split are rarely awarded marks.

## Key terms

- **Asexual reproduction** — production of offspring from one parent without fusion of gametes.
- **Sexual reproduction** — production of offspring by fusion of two gametes.
- **Clone** — a genetically identical copy of an organism or cell.
- **Binary fission** — division of a prokaryotic cell into two identical cells.
- **Budding** — a new organism grows as an outgrowth from the parent and then separates.
- **Fragmentation** — a parent breaks into pieces that each grow into a new organism.
- **Vegetative propagation** — new plants formed from stems, roots or leaves of a parent plant.
- **Parthenogenesis** — development of an embryo from an unfertilised egg.
- **Genetic diversity** — the variety of alleles and allele combinations in a population.
- **Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT)** — cloning by putting the nucleus of a body cell into an enucleated egg.
- **Embryo splitting** — dividing an early embryo to produce identical offspring.

## Summary

- Asexual reproduction uses one parent and produces genetically identical offspring quickly and cheaply.
- Its main types are binary fission, budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagation and parthenogenesis.
- Sexual reproduction is slower and costlier but produces genetically diverse offspring through crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation.
- Genetic diversity increases the chance that some individuals survive environmental change or disease.
- Reproductive cloning, by plant propagation, embryo splitting or SCNT, produces genetically identical organisms for agriculture, horticulture and conservation, but has low success rates in animals and no genetic diversity.

questions.prompt: Which type of asexual reproduction involves a new individual developing as an outgrowth that later detaches from the parent, as seen in yeast?
questions.explanation: Budding produces a small outgrowth that grows and separates, as in yeast and Hydra. Binary fission is tempting, but there the cell splits into two equal halves rather than producing a smaller bud.

options.A: the splitting of a prokaryotic cell into two identical cells.
options.B: the growth of a new plant from a stem or root.
options.C: the fusion of two gametes from the same parent.
options.D: the development of an embryo from an unfertilised egg.

questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis is development from an egg that has not been fertilised. Option C describes self-fertilisation, which still involves fusion of gametes and is therefore sexual reproduction.

questions.prompt: Why is a population that reproduces only asexually more at risk from a new disease than a population that reproduces sexually?

options.A: The individuals are genetically very similar, so if one is susceptible, most or all are likely to be susceptible.
options.B: Asexual organisms do not have immune systems.
options.C: Asexual reproduction produces fewer offspring, so the population is always small.
options.D: Mutations cannot occur in asexually reproducing organisms.

questions.explanation: Clones share the same alleles, so a disease that kills one tends to kill all. Option C is tempting but wrong: asexual reproduction usually produces offspring faster, not fewer.

questions.prompt: Which process in sexual reproduction creates new combinations of alleles on a single chromosome?
questions.explanation: Crossing over swaps sections between homologous chromosomes, producing chromosomes with new allele combinations. Independent assortment is tempting, but it mixes whole chromosomes rather than changing the alleles on any one chromosome.

questions.prompt: A gardener wants many strawberry plants identical to one plant that produces very sweet fruit. Which method is most suitable?

options.A: Planting seeds collected from the sweet plant
options.B: Cross-pollinating the sweet plant with another variety
options.C: Growing new plants from the runners of the sweet plant
options.D: Allowing the plant to self-pollinate and planting the seeds

questions.explanation: Runners are vegetative propagation, which produces clones with the same sweet-fruit genes. Self-pollination (D) is tempting, but meiosis still shuffles alleles, so seedlings may differ from the parent.

questions.prompt: In somatic cell nuclear transfer, a nucleus from a cow with a red coat is put into an enucleated egg from a cow with a black coat, and the embryo is carried by a surrogate with a white coat. Assuming coat colour is controlled by nuclear genes, the calf will most likely have

options.D: a mix of red, black and white.

questions.explanation: The calf's nuclear DNA comes from the red cow, so it will have a red coat. The black cow supplied only the egg cytoplasm and mitochondria; the surrogate supplied only the uterus.

questions.prompt: Aphids reproduce by parthenogenesis in summer when food is plentiful and reproduce sexually in autumn. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.A: Sexual reproduction is faster, which suits the short autumn season.
options.B: Parthenogenesis produces more genetic diversity during summer.
options.C: Aphids cannot find mates during summer.
options.D: Asexual reproduction allows rapid population growth in good conditions, while sexual reproduction produces diverse offspring better able to survive changing conditions.

questions.explanation: This strategy combines the speed of asexual reproduction with the genetic diversity of sexual reproduction when conditions worsen. Option A is wrong because sexual reproduction is slower, not faster.

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 30 minutes. Starting from a single cell, how many cells will there be after 4 hours under ideal conditions?
questions.explanation: 4 hours = 240 minutes, and 240 ÷ 30 = 8 generations, so the number of cells is 2⁸ = 256. A common error is to count 7 or 9 generations, giving 128 or 512.
